statement: Five children queue up. Ana is somewhere ahead of Bo. Cal is behind Bo but ahead of Dee. Eve is last. Who is second in the queue?

choices.misconception: I gave the child who is first rather than the one who is second.
I placed Cal directly after Ana, reading ahead of Dee as meaning immediately ahead.
I built the order backwards from the last position instead of forwards from the first.
I assumed the clues left several orders open without checking that they chain into a single one.

hints: Draw one line and place them on it.
Each clue is a link in a chain. Write the links down as you read them, then see whether they join end to end - if they do, the whole order is fixed.
Ana is before Bo, Bo before Cal, Cal before Dee, and Eve is last. That chains to Ana, Bo, Cal, Dee, Eve - so Bo is second.

solutions.reliable: Turn each clue into a link. Ana before Bo. Cal after Bo but before Dee, so Bo before Cal before Dee. Chaining: Ana, Bo, Cal, Dee. Eve is last, which is the fifth place, and the chain fills the first four exactly. So the order is fully determined and Bo is second. The transferable idea: draw one line and place people on it as the clues arrive - the moment the links chain end to end, the order is fixed.

whyOnTest: Reading before as immediately before is the classic misreading, and it is what makes students think an order is ambiguous when it is not.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
